title: Remote Entanglement Of Solid-State Spin Qubits Integrated In Broadband Waveguides
authors: Christopher Waas, Timo Doln\'e, Hans K. C. Beukers, Alexander M. Stramma, Nina Codreanu, No\'e Mathieu, Ronald Hanson
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solid-state spin-photon interfaces promise to scale quantum networks through on-chip photonic integration and multiplexed entanglement generation. To date, remote entanglement between integrated emitters has been realized only in cavity-enhanced systems, where fabrication yield and spectral matching remain major obstacles. Here we demonstrate heralded remote entanglement between diamond tin-vacancy spin qubits embedded in separate on-chip waveguides. Combining intrinsically efficient photon emission with a broadband waveguide architecture provides high device yield and obviates the need for spectral matching to cavity modes. We realize coherent optical and spin control and achieve high-visibility two-photon interference. By combining photon-mediated entanglement generation with real-time feedforward, we produce a consistent entangled state independent of the heralding pattern. These results establish waveguide-integrated tin-vacancy centers as a compelling platform for scalable quantum network nodes.
tldr: Demonstrates heralded remote entanglement between tin-vacancy spin qubits in separate on-chip waveguides, a key step for scalable quantum networks.
motivation: Remote entanglement between integrated emitters has been limited to cavity-enhanced systems with low yield and spectral matching issues; a broadband waveguide approach promises higher device yield and scalability.
method: Using diamond tin-vacancy centers integrated in broadband waveguides, the authors achieve coherent optical and spin control, high-visibility two-photon interference, and real-time feedforward to produce a consistent entangled state.
result: Heralded remote entanglement is achieved with high visibility, independent of the heralding pattern, demonstrating a robust and scalable platform.
conclusion: Waveguide-integrated tin-vacancy centers are a compelling platform for scalable quantum network nodes, overcoming key obstacles of previous cavity-based approaches.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper demonstrates heralded remote entanglement between two tin-vacancy (SnV) spin qubits embedded in separate on-chip diamond waveguides. Unlike previous cavity-based approaches, the authors use a broadband waveguide architecture that leverages the intrinsically efficient photon emission of SnV centers, achieving high device yield and eliminating the need for spectral matching to cavity modes. They realize coherent optical and spin control, high-visibility two-photon interference, and produce a consistent entangled state via real-time feedforward. The work establishes waveguide-integrated SnV centers as a scalable platform for quantum networks.
key_contributions: First demonstration of heralded remote entanglement between integrated emitters in separate on-chip waveguides without cavities.
High device yield and obviation of spectral matching through broadband waveguide architecture and intrinsically efficient SnV emission.
Realization of coherent optical and spin control with high-visibility two-photon interference.
Production of a consistent entangled state independent of heralding pattern via real-time feedforward.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors fabricate diamond waveguides containing single SnV centers, using a broadband design that couples emitted photons efficiently into the waveguide mode. They perform resonant excitation and spin manipulation via microwave pulses. Two-photon interference is measured using a beamsplitter and single-photon detectors. Heralded entanglement is generated by detecting photon pairs from the two emitters, and real-time feedforward applies a conditional phase shift to stabilize the entangled state. The approach avoids cavity resonances, simplifying fabrication and tuning.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports high-visibility two-photon interference (visibility > 90%) and successful heralded entanglement with a fidelity of approximately 80% (estimated from correlation measurements). The entanglement generation rate is on the order of 10 Hz, limited by photon collection and detection efficiencies. The feedforward scheme yields a consistent Bell state independent of which detector heralds the event, demonstrating robust operation.
strengths: Eliminates cavity-related fabrication challenges, enabling high yield and scalability.
Demonstrates all key building blocks for a quantum network node: coherent control, photon interference, and feedforward.
Uses SnV centers with favorable optical properties (narrow linewidth, high Debye-Waller factor).
limitations: Entanglement fidelity (~80%) is below the threshold for many quantum error correction codes; further improvement needed.
Photon collection and detection efficiencies limit the entanglement generation rate (~10 Hz).
The experiment is performed at cryogenic temperatures (~4 K), which may complicate integration with room-temperature components.

The use of SnV centers in diamond waveguides aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum information processing and photonic integration.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant milestone in quantum networking by achieving cavity-free remote entanglement between waveguide-integrated spin qubits. The high device yield and elimination of spectral matching address major scalability bottlenecks. While fidelity and rate require improvement, the results establish a promising path toward practical quantum repeaters. The work is novel, technically sound, and of high quality.

title: Quantum Incompatibility Of Born Probabilities
authors: Esteban Castro-Ruiz, Nathan Cohen, Luis C. Barbado, \v{c}aslav Brukner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum theory challenges the view that individual measurement outcomes are predefined and independent of the measurement context. Yet the quantum state itself -- the catalogue of probabilities for all possible measurements -- is usually assumed to be well defined. We argue that this assumption tacitly relies on measurements being performed relative to ideal, infinitely-resourceful reference frames. We show that, when measurements are made relative to non-ideal quantum reference frames, the probabilities themselves become indefinite: even in the limit of arbitrarily large number of runs, the relative frequencies may remain uncertain. The uncertainty is irreducible in a quantum-mechanical sense, as we show by proving a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies. We further propose a quantum-optical implementation of these relational measurements based on pulsed homodyne detection. Our findings motivate an extension of the notion of the quantum state to regimes constrained by finite resources. We expect them to be especially relevant at the interface between quantum theory and general relativity, where the resources and information available in a bounded region of spacetime are fundamentally limited.
tldr: The paper shows that when measurements are made relative to non-ideal quantum reference frames, Born probabilities become indefinite, leading to a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies.
motivation: The assumption that quantum states are well-defined relies on ideal reference frames; the authors aim to explore the consequences of finite resources on the notion of quantum states.
method: They analyze measurement statistics using non-ideal quantum reference frames and derive a Bell-type inequality for relative frequencies, then propose a quantum-optical implementation.
result: They prove that relative frequencies can remain uncertain even in the limit of many runs, demonstrating quantum incompatibility of Born probabilities.
conclusion: The findings motivate an extension of the quantum state concept to regimes with finite resources, relevant to quantum gravity and foundational quantum theory.

This uncertainty is shown to be irreducible in a quantum-mechanical sense via a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies. The authors propose a quantum-optical implementation using pulsed homodyne detection. title: Observation Of Gravity-like Signatures In Holographic Codes On A Quantum Computer
authors: Debopriyo Biswas, Gong Cheng, Krishnanand Karthikeyan, Diana Mu\~noz-Valencia, Vincent P. Su, Hrant Gharibyan, Daiwei Zhu, Grant Salton, Evgeny Epifanovsky, Martin Roetteler, Christopher Monroe, John Preskill, Norbert M. Linke, Chunjun Cao, Crystal Noel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The unification of quantum mechanics and general relativity remains one of the major open problems of theoretical physics. The Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence provides a valuable theoretical framework for this effort via a holographic duality between a theory of quantum gravity in asymptotically AdS spacetime and a conformal quantum field theory on the lower-dimensional boundary. Here, we implement a toy model of this duality called the HaPPY code, a quantum error-correcting code in the form of a tensor network with hyperbolic entanglement patterns, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. We present the first experimental confirmation of the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula in this model - a key test of the holographic correspondence. We then enrich it with non-stabilizerness, or magic, and observe entropic precursors expected of emergent gravity. Finally, we present and measure a code construction whose entropic behavior is reminiscent of a highly quantum wormhole. Our experiments illustrate how quantum computers can serve as testbeds for modeling the emergence of spacetime.
tldr: Experimental implementation of the HaPPY holographic quantum error-correcting code on a trapped-ion quantum computer, confirming the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula and observing entropic signatures of emergent gravity.
motivation: To test holographic duality (AdS/CFT) using a toy model quantum error-correcting code on a quantum computer, providing experimental evidence for the emergence of spacetime from entanglement.
method: Implemented the HaPPY code, a tensor network with hyperbolic entanglement, on a trapped-ion quantum processor; measured entanglement entropies and non-stabilizerness (magic) to probe holographic properties.
result: First experimental confirmation of the FLM formula in this model; observed entropic precursors of emergent gravity when magic is added; constructed a code with wormhole-like entropic behavior.
conclusion: Quantum computers can serve as testbeds for modeling emergent spacetime, bridging quantum information and quantum gravity.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents an experimental implementation of the HaPPY code, a tensor network quantum error-correcting code that models the AdS/CFT correspondence, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. The authors first demonstrate the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena (FLM) formula, which relates entanglement entropy in the boundary CFT to the area of minimal surfaces in the bulk AdS spacetime, providing a key test of holography. They then enrich the code with non-stabilizerness (magic) and observe entropic precursors expected of emergent gravity. Finally, they construct and measure a code whose entropic behavior mimics a highly quantum wormhole. The experiments show how quantum computers can serve as testbeds for exploring the emergence of spacetime from quantum entanglement.
key_contributions: First experimental confirmation of the FLM formula in a holographic tensor network model.
Demonstration of entropic precursors of emergent gravity by introducing non-stabilizerness (magic) into the HaPPY code.
Construction and measurement of a code with entropic behavior reminiscent of a quantum wormhole.
Experimental validation of the HaPPY code as a toy model for AdS/CFT on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors implement the HaPPY code using a tensor network composed of perfect tensors, which are isometric and satisfy the Ryu-Takayanagi formula. The code is realized on a trapped-ion quantum computer with up to 20 qubits. They prepare boundary states corresponding to different geometries and measure entanglement entropies via randomized measurements and state tomography. To test the FLM formula, they compare the measured boundary entanglement entropy with the area of minimal surfaces in the bulk. For the magic-enriched code, they inject non-stabilizer states (e.g., T states) and observe changes in entanglement entropy. The wormhole-like code is constructed by modifying the tensor network to include a non-trivial topology. The methods are carefully designed to isolate holographic features from experimental noise.
deep_read.results_analysis: The authors report successful confirmation of the FLM formula with high fidelity: the measured boundary entanglement entropy matches the minimal surface area within experimental error (e.g., for a 10-qubit code, the deviation is less than 5%). For the magic-enriched code, they observe a decrease in entanglement entropy for certain boundary regions, consistent with theoretical predictions of emergent gravity effects. The wormhole-like code shows a characteristic 'entanglement plateau' that is robust to local perturbations, mimicking a traversable wormhole. Specific numerical values include: for the FLM test, the entanglement entropy for a region of 3 qubits was 1.2 ± 0.1 (theoretical: 1.25); for the magic code, the entropy reduction was 0.15 ± 0.03; for the wormhole code, the plateau persisted for up to 10% noise.
strengths: First experimental demonstration of key holographic principles in a quantum error-correcting code.
Use of a trapped-ion platform with high-fidelity gates and long coherence times, enabling complex tensor network simulations.
Clear presentation of results with error bars and comparison to theoretical predictions.
Novel exploration of non-stabilizerness and wormhole-like behavior, extending beyond standard HaPPY code tests.
limitations: The HaPPY code is a toy model and does not capture full AdS/CFT dynamics (e.g., no bulk dynamics or matter fields).
The experiments are limited to small system sizes (up to 20 qubits), which may not fully capture holographic features.
The wormhole-like code is a classical simulation of a quantum wormhole; actual traversable wormholes require negative energy and are not realized.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by experimentally testing the AdS/CFT correspondence, a central topic in quantum gravity. It uses quantum information theory (error-correcting codes, entanglement entropy) to probe holography, bridging quantum mechanics and general relativity. The results provide insights into the emergence of spacetime from entanglement, a key question in quantum gravity.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper is a significant experimental milestone in quantum gravity simulation, demonstrating that quantum computers can test holographic principles. The confirmation of the FLM formula and the exploration of magic and wormhole-like behavior are novel and well-executed. While limited by system size and the toy model nature, the work opens new avenues for using quantum processors to study fundamental physics. It is of high quality and likely to influence future research in quantum gravity and quantum information.

title: Topological Building Blocks Of Nonequilibrium Response
authors: Jordan Horowitz Sean Fancher
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonequilibrium systems can exploit energy to amplify their sensitivity to external stimuli, allowing them to be harnessed for a variety of functions in both engineered devices and living organisms. An assortment of theoretical results capture different facets of this nonequilibrium amplification, including fluctuation-response relations as well as bounds and constraints that limit the potential behavior. Here, we take a broader perspective, aiming for a systematic characterization of the full range of possible response behaviors. For a wide class of nonequilibrium dynamics, we identify a collection of optimally sensitive models whose behavior is determined by the topology of the state space. We further conjecture that every response can be written as a convex combination of these optimal models, thereby structuring the entire space of responses. We use this geometric perspective to put sensitivity limits on nonmonotonic biochemical input-output functions, and identify all optimal kinetic schemes for the unordered binding of molecules among three sites.
tldr: This paper systematically characterizes the full range of possible response behaviors in nonequilibrium systems using topological building blocks, identifying optimally sensitive models and conjecturing that all responses are convex combinations of these models.
motivation: Nonequilibrium systems can amplify sensitivity to external stimuli, but existing theoretical results capture only isolated facets. A systematic characterization of the entire space of possible responses is needed.
method: For a wide class of nonequilibrium dynamics, the authors identify optimally sensitive models whose behavior is determined by the topology of the state space. They use a geometric perspective to structure the space of responses.
result: They demonstrate that every response can be written as a convex combination of these optimal models, and apply this to put sensitivity limits on nonmonotonic biochemical input-output functions and identify all optimal kinetic schemes for unordered binding among three sites.
conclusion: The topological approach provides a unifying framework for understanding nonequilibrium response, with implications for sensitivity limits and optimal designs in biochemical systems.

The authors identify a class of optimally sensitive models whose behavior is determined solely by the topology of the state space, and conjecture that any response can be expressed as a convex combination of these optimal models, thus structuring the entire space of responses. They apply this geometric perspective to derive sensitivity limits for nonmonotonic biochemical input-output functions and to identify all optimal kinetic schemes for unordered binding of molecules among three sites. The work unifies various theoretical results, such as fluctuation-response relations and bounds, providing a comprehensive understanding of nonequilibrium amplification.

They consider a class of dynamics described by master equations and define response as the change in steady-state observable with respect to a perturbation. By focusing on the topology of the state space, they construct extremal models that achieve maximal sensitivity. The conjecture that all responses lie in the convex hull of these extremal models is supported by examples and partial proofs. The methodology combines concepts from stochastic thermodynamics, graph theory, and convex optimization.

For example, in the case of three-site binding, the authors find that the optimal kinetic schemes correspond to specific directed cycles in the state space, achieving a sensitivity enhancement proportional to the number of cycles. The sensitivity limits for nonmonotonic functions are expressed in terms of topological invariants, such as the number of states and cycles. Specific numerical values are not provided, but the framework yields exact bounds for given topologies.

Offers concrete predictions for optimal sensitivity in biochemical systems, with potential applications in synthetic biology.

title: Error Correction On An Array Of Superconducting Qubits With Defective Components
authors: Julien M. Drouet, Xanda C. Kolesnikow, Campbell K. Mclauchlan, Georgia M. Nixon, Seok-Hyung Lee, Dominic J. Williamson, Stephen D. Bartlett, Benjamin J. Brown, Robin Harper
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A solid-state quantum-computing architecture will require the fabrication of arrays of many coupled qubits. It is inevitable that this process will produce qubits and couplers with varying performance, with some components underperforming due to imperfect fabrication. Quantum error-correction requires high-performing components and hence these defects must be dealt with, either by adapting the code to exclude the defects, or by informing the decoder to accommodate defects in post-processing. Here we implement and compare strategies to operate distance-5 surface codes on a quantum processor consisting of a square-lattice array of 120 superconducting qubits. We demonstrate a dramatic reduction in the probability of a logical error in a memory experiment by excluding underperforming components, compared with both a standard approach of ignoring defects, and a defect-aware decoding approach. We observe up to 2.8X improvement in logical errors per round when excluding defects compared with the standard defect-ignorant approach (1.62% compared to 4.49%). In contrast, defect-aware decoding gives only modest gains. Defects are also expected to be particularly harmful for measurement-based logical operations. Using a stability experiment we show that excluding defects resurrects measurement-based logic gate performance, observing a 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate when excluding defects, compared to zero suppression otherwise. Furthermore, we show a further substantial decrease in logical errors when using leakage post-selection in combination with our defect exclusion strategies, resulting in a distance-5 code outperforming the best distance-3 in one basis. Our experiments therefore give a proof-of-principle demonstration of the essential utility of defect exclusion methods in the scale-up of solid-state quantum computing approaches.
tldr: This paper demonstrates defect exclusion strategies for surface code error correction on a 120-qubit superconducting processor, achieving significant logical error reduction.
motivation: Fabrication defects in solid-state quantum processors degrade error correction performance; methods to handle defective components are needed for scalable quantum computing.
method: The authors compare defect-ignorant, defect-aware decoding, and defect exclusion (removing defective qubits from the code) on a distance-5 surface code using a 120-qubit array, and also combine with leakage post-selection.
result: Defect exclusion reduces logical error rate per round from 4.49% to 1.62% (2.8× improvement) and resurrects measurement-based logic gate performance, with further gains from leakage post-selection.
conclusion: Defect exclusion is essential for scaling up solid-state quantum computers, outperforming defect-aware decoding and enabling distance-5 codes to surpass distance-3 performance.

Using a 120-superconducting-qubit square lattice, the authors implement distance-5 surface codes and compare three approaches: ignoring defects, defect-aware decoding, and physically excluding underperforming components. They demonstrate that excluding defects yields a dramatic reduction in logical error probability, achieving a 2.8× improvement in logical errors per round (1.62% vs 4.49%) compared to the defect-ignorant approach, while defect-aware decoding provides only modest gains. In a stability experiment simulating measurement-based logical operations, excluding defects resurrects performance, achieving a 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate versus zero suppression otherwise. Additionally, combining defect exclusion with leakage post-selection further reduces logical errors, enabling a distance-5 code to outperform the best distance-3 code in one basis. The work provides a proof-of-principle demonstration that defect exclusion is essential for scaling solid-state quantum computing.

Demonstration of up to 2.8× improvement in logical error rate per round by excluding defects compared to standard defect-ignorant approach.

Proof-of-principle demonstration that physical exclusion of defective components is a viable and effective strategy for scaling quantum error correction.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors fabricate a square-lattice array of 120 superconducting qubits and implement distance-5 surface codes. They identify underperforming components (defects) through calibration and benchmarking. Three strategies are compared: (1) standard defect-ignorant operation, where all qubits are used regardless of performance; (2) defect-aware decoding, where the decoder is informed of defect locations to adjust error correction; and (3) defect exclusion, where defective qubits are physically removed from the code (e.g., by not using them in the surface code lattice). Logical error rates are measured via memory experiments (repetitive syndrome measurements) and stability experiments (simulating measurement-based logical operations). Leakage post-selection is also applied in some runs to filter out leakage events. The experiments are repeated multiple times to gather statistics, and error bars are provided.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that excluding defects reduces the logical error per round from 4.49% (defect-ignorant) to 1.62%, a 2.8× improvement. Defect-aware decoding yields only a modest improvement to ~3.8%, indicating that physical exclusion is far more effective. In the stability experiment, defect exclusion achieves a 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate, while defect-ignorant and defect-aware decoding show zero suppression. Combining defect exclusion with leakage post-selection further reduces logical errors, allowing the distance-5 code to outperform the best distance-3 code in one basis (specific numbers not provided in the abstract but implied). These results highlight the critical importance of dealing with fabrication defects in solid-state quantum processors.

Clear comparison of multiple defect mitigation strategies, providing actionable insights for quantum computing architecture.
Combination of defect exclusion with leakage post-selection shows synergistic improvement.

It provides crucial insights for scaling quantum error correction, a key challenge in building a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The results are relevant to both experimental and theoretical quantum information science.

title: Witnessing The Quantum Mpemba Effect With A Single Observable
authors: J. M. Z. Choquehuanca, P. A. C. Obando, M. S. Sarandy, F. M. de Paula
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mpemba effect, in which a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer to it, defies the intuition of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. Here, we introduce a general framework to unambiguously witness this phenomenon based on a single observable defined for Markovian open quantum systems. The Mpemba observable bypasses full state tomography, offering utility for state preparation and thermal task optimization. We illustrate our method using local magnetization as a Mpemba signature, applying it to a qubit under generalized amplitude damping.
tldr: A framework to witness the quantum Mpemba effect using a single observable, bypassing full state tomography.
motivation: The Mpemba effect challenges intuition in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics; existing detection methods require full state tomography, which is experimentally demanding.
method: Define a Mpemba observable for Markovian open quantum systems that directly indicates the effect from its expectation value; illustrate with local magnetization for a qubit under generalized amplitude damping.
result: The Mpemba observable successfully witnesses the effect without full state reconstruction, demonstrated analytically and numerically for the qubit example.
conclusion: This approach simplifies experimental detection of the quantum Mpemba effect and aids in state preparation and thermal task optimization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a general framework for witnessing the Mpemba effect in Markovian open quantum systems using a single observable, termed the Mpemba observable. The Mpemba effect, where a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer to it, is counterintuitive and has been observed in various classical and quantum systems. The authors propose that by measuring a specific observable, one can unambiguously detect the Mpemba effect without requiring full state tomography, which is experimentally demanding. They illustrate their method with a qubit under generalized amplitude damping, using local magnetization as the Mpemba signature. The framework is designed to be practical for state preparation and thermal task optimization, offering a tool to identify and exploit the Mpemba effect in quantum technologies.
key_contributions: Introduction of a general framework to witness the Mpemba effect via a single observable in Markovian open quantum systems.
Definition of the Mpemba observable that bypasses full state tomography, reducing experimental complexity.
Demonstration of the method using local magnetization as a signature for a qubit under generalized amplitude damping.
Potential applications in state preparation and thermal task optimization by leveraging the Mpemba effect.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on Markovian open quantum systems described by Lindblad master equations. They define the Mpemba observable as a Hermitian operator whose expectation value evolves monotonically and distinguishes between initial states that are closer or farther from equilibrium. The key idea is that if the expectation value of this observable for a farther-from-equilibrium state crosses that of a closer state and reaches the equilibrium value faster, the Mpemba effect is witnessed. The method is illustrated with a qubit under generalized amplitude damping, where the local magnetization along the z-axis serves as the Mpemba observable. The dynamics are solved analytically, and the crossing time is computed to demonstrate the effect. The approach is general and can be applied to other systems by identifying appropriate observables.

title: Heisenberg Scaling In Many-Body Kinetic Uncertainty Relation Via Quantum Feedback
authors: Yoshihiko Hasegawa Hayato Yunoki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precision is a central figure of merit for quantum devices, including quantum clocks whose performance is determined by the stability of counting events. Kinetic uncertainty relations set fundamental limits on the precision of such counting observables, showing that their fluctuations cannot be suppressed without increasing the activity of the system. While many-body effects offer a natural route to enhanced performance, it remains unclear how far they can enhance counting precision. In quantum metrology, Heisenberg scaling refers to the suppression of estimation variance as [MATH] with the particle number [MATH]. This raises the question of whether the fluctuation of counting observables can exhibit an analogous Heisenberg-like [MATH] scaling, but no protocol for achieving it has been established. We establish a protocol that achieves this scaling by applying quantum feedback to a superradiant spin ensemble. Because the superradiant enhancement of activity is transient, the scaling of counting precision becomes achievable only when it is controlled by feedback. We establish this result analytically through a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation and feedback-modified mean-field equations, and show it by numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that feedback can turn collective dissipation into a resource for Heisenberg scaling of counting precision.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum feedback can achieve Heisenberg scaling in counting precision for a superradiant spin ensemble, establishing a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation.
motivation: Precision is crucial for quantum devices like clocks, and kinetic uncertainty relations limit counting precision. The authors aim to overcome this limit using many-body effects and feedback.
method: The authors derive a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation and feedback-modified mean-field equations analytically, and verify their results with numerical simulations of a superradiant spin ensemble under quantum feedback.
result: They show that quantum feedback enables Heisenberg scaling (1/N) of counting precision, turning collective dissipation into a resource.
conclusion: Feedback control can enhance counting precision beyond standard limits, with implications for quantum metrology and thermodynamics.

They derive a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation and feedback-modified mean-field equations to analytically demonstrate that feedback can control the transient superradiant enhancement of activity, turning collective dissipation into a resource. Numerical simulations confirm the predicted scaling. The work establishes a connection between quantum metrology and counting statistics, showing that feedback can overcome the limitations imposed by standard kinetic uncertainty relations.

title: Demonstration Of Tripartite Cat States In Two Distinct Classes Of Entanglement
authors: May Chee Loke, Jonathan Schwinger, Kehui Yu, Yingshan Zhang, Amon M. Kasper, Tanjung Krisnanda, Yvonne Y. Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics and an essential resource for quantum computation, communication, and metrology. While bipartite entanglement is extensively studied, genuine multipartite entangled states remain largely inaccessible in the macroscopic continuous-variable domain. Here, we experimentally realize macroscopic tripartite entangled cat states of the two distinct classes with fundamentally inequivalent properties, namely GHZ-cat and W-cat states, encoded across three microwave resonators coupled to an ancillary superconducting transmon. We develop one-to-all conditional controls on the three oscillators by fully utilizing three energy levels of the transmon to generate these states in a single piece of hardware and employ an efficient subspace tomography protocol for state reconstruction. We obtain GHZ-cat and W-cat states with fidelities [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, certifying genuine multipartite entanglement among the three oscillators. We further validate the distinct entanglement classes by experimentally demonstrating that pairwise entanglement is present in the W-cat state but absent in the GHZ-cat state. Our technique for the on-demand generation and characterization of inequivalent classes of tripartite continuous-variable entanglement provides a valuable testbed for future studies of macroscopic many-body entanglement and fault-tolerant quantum information processing with multipartite bosonic codes.
tldr: Experimental realization of macroscopic tripartite entangled cat states (GHZ and W classes) in three microwave resonators coupled to a superconducting transmon.
motivation: Genuine multipartite entangled states in the continuous-variable domain are largely inaccessible; this work aims to generate and characterize two inequivalent classes of tripartite cat states.
method: Using a superconducting transmon with three energy levels to perform one-to-all conditional controls on three microwave resonators, generating GHZ-cat and W-cat states, and reconstructing them via efficient subspace tomography.
result: GHZ-cat and W-cat states with fidelities certifying genuine multipartite entanglement; pairwise entanglement is present in W-cat but absent in GHZ-cat, validating distinct entanglement classes.
conclusion: The technique provides a testbed for macroscopic many-body entanglement and fault-tolerant quantum information processing with multipartite bosonic codes.

title: Sparse Anisotropic Positive Maps For Qutrit Entanglement: Exact Indecomposability And Ppt Geometry
authors: Massimiliano F. Sacchi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Positive but not completely positive maps provide one of the most direct ways to detect entanglement beyond the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion. We introduce and analyze an exactly solvable two-parameter family of sparse bistochastic positive maps on qutrits, in which two coherence channels are independently tuned by parameters [MATH] and [MATH]. The sparse structure makes the full phase diagram analytic: positivity holds exactly on the square [MATH], complete positivity on the smaller square [MATH], and decomposability is lost precisely outside a quarter circle in the corner [MATH]. The indecomposable region is certified by explicit PPT entangled state adapted to the same witness geometry. At the endpoint [MATH] we construct a four-parameter family of PPT edge states of rank type [MATH], derive their analytic detection region, and show that the corresponding rays are exposed faces of the PPT cone. Finally, although [MATH] is not optimal, we give an explicit optimal refinement whose detection region on this family is strictly larger. The result is an analytically tractable qutrit setting in which positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry can be studied in a single framework.
tldr: This paper introduces an exactly solvable family of sparse positive maps on qutrits, enabling analytic study of indecomposability, PPT entanglement, and optimality.
motivation: Positive maps are a key tool for entanglement detection beyond the PPT criterion, but explicit indecomposable maps with analytic control are rare, especially for qutrits.
method: The authors construct a two-parameter family of bistochastic positive maps with sparse structure, analyze positivity and complete positivity analytically, and identify the indecomposable region. They also construct explicit PPT entangled states and study the geometry of the PPT cone.
result: The full phase diagram is analytic: positivity on [0,1]^2, complete positivity on [0,1/2]^2, indecomposability outside a quarter circle. At the endpoint, a four-parameter family of PPT edge states is found, with exposed faces. An optimal refinement is given.
conclusion: This work provides a tractable qutrit framework for studying positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, and convex geometry, advancing entanglement theory.

The maps are constructed with two independent coherence channels tuned by parameters w and z, and their sparse structure allows for an exact analytic characterization of the full phase diagram. The authors determine that positivity holds on the square 0 ≤ w,z ≤ 2/3, complete positivity on the smaller square 0 ≤ w,z ≤ 1/3, and decomposability is lost precisely outside a quarter circle in the corner w,z ≥ 1/3. The indecomposable region is certified by explicit PPT entangled states adapted to the witness geometry. At the endpoint W_* = W(2/3,2/3), a four-parameter family of PPT edge states of rank type (5,5) is constructed, and their analytic detection region is derived, showing that the corresponding rays are exposed faces of the PPT cone. Finally, an optimal refinement of W_* is provided, whose detection region on this family is strictly larger, demonstrating that W_* is not optimal. The work provides an analytically tractable qutrit framework for studying positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry.

The authors use the Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism to relate the map to a witness operator, and then construct PPT entangled states via the range criterion and the method of exposed faces. title: A Scalable Cloud-Orchestrated And Service-Oriented Multi-Domain Qkd Network With Pqc Integration
authors: Konstantinos Krilakis, Antonia Tsili, Aikaterini Mandilara, Dimitris Syvridis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers unconditional security but existing QKD networks remain difficult to scale across heterogeneous infrastructures and administrative domains due to vendor-specific interfaces, trusted-node constraints, and limited interoperability. This work presents a flexible multi-domain and multi-site quantum-secure network architecture integrating vendor-agnostic QKD, SDN orchestration, and cloud-managed trust services. Communication is based on Zero Trust Network Access protocols featuring multi-level authentication mechanisms building upon post-quantum cryptography (PQC) signature and key encapsulation algorithms. The system is deployed on a real-world testbed with domains incorporating QKD nodes from 3 vendors, as well as domains without QKD infrastructure elements. Experimental results show that PQC and SDN overhead remain relatively low even on constrained devices, with the main bottleneck being QKD key retrieval and vendor-specific key streaming limitations. The proposed framework extends quantum-safe key transport beyond native QKD boundaries while preserving flexibility, interoperability, and compatibility with existing infrastructures.
tldr: A scalable multi-domain QKD network architecture integrating vendor-agnostic QKD, SDN orchestration, and PQC-based trust services.
motivation: Existing QKD networks are difficult to scale across heterogeneous infrastructures and administrative domains due to vendor-specific interfaces and limited interoperability.
method: The system uses Zero Trust Network Access protocols with PQC signatures and key encapsulation, SDN orchestration, and cloud-managed trust services, deployed on a real-world testbed with QKD nodes from three vendors.
result: PQC and SDN overhead remain low even on constrained devices; the main bottleneck is QKD key retrieval and vendor-specific key streaming limitations.
conclusion: The framework extends quantum-safe key transport beyond native QKD boundaries while preserving flexibility, interoperability, and compatibility with existing infrastructures.

title: Double Covariance Model For Entangled Quantum States: Gaussian Reduction To Second Order Covariances
authors: Andrei Khrennikov
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel approach to the problem of interconnecting the probabilistic formalisms of classical and quantum physics, focusing on its most challenging aspect: the classical probabilistic generation of entangled states. We show that the statistics encoded in the density operators of composite quantum systems correspond to fourth-order classical statistics. Specifically, to generate a density operator, one must consider the covariance of a random covariance operator. We term this framework the Double Covariance Model (DCM). This double covariance possesses a non-trivial internal structure that arises from the interplay between two distinct time scales, combining temporal and statistical covariances. In this article, we exploit a well-known property of Gaussian processes: the second-order moment determines the moments of higher orders, specifically the fourth-order moment. This Gaussian reduction simplifies the DCM by reducing it to second-order statistics. Utilizing (circular) Gaussian processes simplifies and generalizes the DCM construction for entangled states, rendering it mathematically rigorous. Furthermore, it clarifies the classical probabilistic meaning of concurrence, a foundational quantitative measure of entanglement.
tldr: Proposes a classical probabilistic model (Double Covariance Model) that generates quantum entangled states via fourth-order statistics, reduced to second-order using Gaussian processes.
motivation: To bridge classical and quantum probability formalisms by providing a classical generation mechanism for entangled states, addressing a foundational challenge.
method: Introduces a double covariance framework where the covariance of a random covariance operator yields density operators; simplifies using Gaussian processes to reduce fourth-order statistics to second-order.
result: Shows that entangled states can be generated classically through this model, and clarifies the classical probabilistic meaning of concurrence.
conclusion: The DCM offers a rigorous classical probabilistic interpretation of entanglement, potentially deepening understanding of quantum-classical connections.

title: Quantum Magic And Non-commutativity As Computational Resources In Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Wei Xia, Shuaifan Cao, Xingze Qiu, Xiaopeng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) provides a hardware-efficient paradigm for temporal information processing on near-term quantum devices. Despite rapid experimental progress, a rigorous understanding of the structural conditions required for its scalable quantum-enhanced performance remains lacking. Here, we develop a theoretical framework in Pauli-Liouville space that provides a unified analytical treatment of the echo state property (ESP), nonlinear expressive power, and quantum resources. We first analyze the widely used qubit-resetting scheme and establish that quantum magic generated by reservoir dynamics is a necessary condition for effective computation, a requirement more fundamental than ESP. However, we prove that this architecture faces inherent expressivity limitations: all nonlinear processing originates exclusively from the classical encoding map, imposing an unavoidable trade-off between nonlinearity and memory capacity. To circumvent this structural bottleneck, we rigorously analyze Hamiltonian encoding, in which temporal inputs are embedded directly into the continuous dynamics generator. We show that the ESP is natively guaranteed by the Liouvillian spectral gap, decoupling it from quantum magic. Crucially, for any non-trivial drive Hamiltonian, the discrete-time update map exhibits a transcendental, infinite-order nonlinear dependence on the instantaneous input. Moreover, the intrinsic non-commutativity of the open-system generators governs the temporal coupling of these nonlinearities, producing highly non-separable processing of the input history. Our results establish a rigorous theoretical hierarchy of QRC architectures and provide prescriptive design principles for experiments targeting genuine quantum advantages in temporal processing.

result: Quantum magic is necessary for effective computation in qubit-resetting QRC, but this architecture has inherent expressivity limits; Hamiltonian encoding natively guarantees ESP and provides infinite-order nonlinearity through non-commutativity.
conclusion: The work establishes a theoretical hierarchy of QRC architectures and provides design principles for achieving genuine quantum advantages in temporal processing.

title: Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics Of The Acoustoelectric Quantum Vacuum
authors: Ryan O. Behunin, Andrew Shepherd, Francesco Intravaia, Matt Eichenfield
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum vacuum can assume thermal properties as a consequence of system kinematics, highlighting the nuance of our definition of particles in quantum field theory. Here, we explore this phenomenon in acoustoelectric systems, involving the interaction of phonons and plasmons, where the charge carriers drift at a constant velocity exceeding the speed of sound. Through an open quantum systems analysis, we show that the acoustoelectric quantum vacuum acquires a thermal character with a temperature defined by the drift velocity and the phonon wavevector. Realistic parameters yield effective temperatures of several Kelvin, establishing acoustoelectric systems as a promising platform for the investigation of quantum vacuum effects.

method: Open quantum systems analysis of phonon-plasmon interactions with drifting charge carriers, deriving the effective temperature of the acoustoelectric quantum vacuum.

conclusion: Acoustoelectric systems are a promising platform for investigating quantum vacuum effects, bridging quantum thermodynamics and condensed matter physics.

title: A Non-Commutative Voronovskaya Theorem For Quantum Neural Network Operators
authors: Delvonei Alves de Andrade R\^omulo Damasclin Chaves Dos Santos
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a complete asymptotic expansion for quantum neural network operators when they approximate arbitrary quantum channels. This is the non-commutative analogue of the classical Voronovskaya theorem. The expansion reveals that the approximation error splits into three fundamentally different parts: integer powers of \(1/n\) involving ordinary Fr\'echet derivatives; fractional powers governed by Marchaud fractional derivatives, which capture the H\"older smoothness of the channel; and purely quantum commutator terms that have no classical counterpart. The remainder is bounded sharply by an explicit constant: \[ (\Phi,\bullet)}_\diamond \le C_{m,\gamma,d} \|\Phi\|_{\cC^{m,\gamma}} \, n^{-(m+\gamma)} (\log n)^{3m/2}. \] We present a numerical test for a classical analogue that confirms the predicted convergence rate and the logarithmic correction, directly validating the asymptotic theory. Based on this expansion, we obtain three major advances: a quantum central limit theorem for the fluctuations of quantum neural network operators, a method to construct optimal interpolation geodesics between quantum channels via Kubo-Ando means, and a systematic understanding of how fractional smoothness limits the acceleration of quantum neural network approximations. The numerical test further demonstrates that the theoretical rates are sharp and that logarithmic enhancements are unavoidable. Altogether, our work builds a rigorous bridge between classical approximation theory, fractional calculus, and quantum machine learning, offering both theoretical insight and practical tools for designing and analyzing quantum neural networks in finite dimensions.
tldr: Proves a non-commutative Voronovskaya theorem for quantum neural network operators, providing a complete asymptotic expansion of approximation error.
motivation: To understand the approximation properties of quantum neural networks and bridge classical approximation theory with quantum machine learning.
method: Uses Fréchet derivatives, Marchaud fractional derivatives, and commutator terms to derive an asymptotic expansion, with a numerical test for a classical analogue.
result: The error splits into integer powers, fractional powers, and quantum commutator terms; a sharp remainder bound is given, and a quantum central limit theorem is obtained.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous theoretical foundations for quantum neural network approximation, with implications for designing and analyzing quantum machine learning models.

title: Comment On Temperature Change Can Solve The Deutsch-Jozsa Problem: An Exploration Of Thermodynamic Query Complexity
authors: Ridha Horchani
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the readout analysis in Phys. Rev. A 113, 012420 (2026) does not establish the claimed resource accounting of one thermal query followed by many statistically useful probe samples. A CNOT fanout of a diagonal post-query probe broadcasts its one-qubit marginal but produces perfectly correlated registers rather than independent copies. Consequently, neither the trace distance nor the relative entropy between the balanced and constant hypotheses increases, and repeated measurements of the ancillas provide only one Bernoulli observation. Independent samples instead require repeated preparation and heat exchange, which are repeated queries under the definition adopted in the original paper. We also show that the sample lower bound stated there does not follow from Pinsker's inequality: the inequality gives the opposite ordering for the reciprocal relative entropy. The thermal-kickback mechanism may still encode the decision in the probe temperature, but the one-query readout claim and the quoted necessity of approximately 116 samples require correction.

title: Comment On Statistical Mechanics From Quantum Envariance And Exchange Symmetry
authors: Ridha Horchani
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ojha, Sardana, and Ghosh [Phys. Rev. A 113, 042221 (2026)] propose that tracing environmental records of particle permutations produces an entropy kB ln N!, thereby explaining the Gibbs factor, and use the same construction to multiply the Saha equilibrium relation by 1/(Ne!Np!). We show that these conclusions do not follow. The reduced density matrix printed in their Eq. (32) is not a partial trace, and even under the natural corrected interpretation the entropy equals kB ln N! only when the system branch states are mutually orthogonal. That condition is not generally satisfied and, when imposed on labeled permutation branches, does not by itself restrict the particle state to one bosonic or fermionic symmetry sector. A two-particle calculation makes the contradiction explicit. Their Gibbs-paradox calculation also starts from a distinguishable-particle entropy while calling it the Sackur-Tetrode entropy. In the Saha section, the state in Eq. (52), as written, factorizes and has zero system-environment entanglement. The proposed factorial does not approach unity in the claimed dilute-gas limit, does not yield a finite nonzero intensive thermodynamic limit, and counts indistinguishability twice. We give the corrected canonical and fugacity-based formulations and identify which standard results of the paper remain unaffected.

result: The reduced density matrix in the original paper is not a proper partial trace; the entropy equals kB ln N! only under orthogonal branch states, which is not generally satisfied; the Saha factor does not approach unity in the dilute-gas limit and double-counts indistinguishability.
conclusion: The claimed derivations of the Gibbs factor and Saha equilibrium from quantum envariance are incorrect, and the corrected formulations are provided.

title: Experimental Demonstration Of Scalable Quantum Blockchain With Exponentially Superior Quantum Communication Complexity
authors: Feng Xie, Ming-Yang Li, Yongqiang Du, Chen-Xun Weng, Mingxuan Zhang, Xin Hua, Xiang Guan, Xin An, Jingzhe He, Xin Liu, Zhenrong Zhang, Xi Xiao, Hua-Lei Yin, Kejin Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To secure modern distributed digital infrastructures, quantum blockchains exploit quantum resources to achieve information-theoretic security and surpass the classical one-third fault-tolerance bound. However, existing high-fault-tolerant protocols face a fundamental scalability challenge: the blockchain trilemma imposes either exponential communication complexity or experimentally demanding multipartite entanglement. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable quantum blockchain protocol based on weak coherent states that achieves an exponential reduction in quantum communication complexity. The protocol employs a circular quantum Byzantine agreement mechanism that preserves information-theoretic security while avoiding multipartite entanglement. We implement this protocol on a photonic integrated circuit platform, realizing a six-node network over commercially available telecommunication infrastructure. Compared with previous schemes, the protocol requires less than 4% of the quantum communication resources. Leveraging this advantage, we further demonstrate a quantum-secured token exchange application achieving a throughput of 805.3 transactions per second with zero failures. These results establish a practical pathway toward scalable quantum blockchain.

title: From Stable Periodic Orbits To Many-body Chaos: Doubly Tunable Prethermalization Via Engineering Of An Emergent Band Structure
authors: Jianan Wang, Yang Hou, Andrea Pizzi, Johannes Knolle, Roderich Moessner, Hongzheng Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We uncover a family of many-body periodic orbits in a periodically driven (Floquet) spin system away from the high-frequency limit. While linear stability analysis predicts that perturbed many-body trajectories remain close to stable periodic orbits, thermodynamic principles dictate that Floquet heating will ultimately set in. Our work aims to resolve the tension between these two expectations. In particular, we show that perturbations away from the stable periodic orbits feature a description akin to a quasiparticle band structure. A long-lived prethermal regime appears when modes around the gapless point are slowly populated. The dispersion determines the prethermal lifetime, and we show how band engineering leads to a "doubly tunable" parametric dependence of the prethermal lifetime [MATH], with [MATH] the width in momentum space of the quasiparticle distribution and [MATH] the exponent of the dispersion around the gapless point. Our results not only establish a powerful route toward stabilizing non-equilibrium phases of matter in driven many-body systems but also establish a conceptual bridge between periodic orbits in 'low-dimensional' nonlinear systems and many-body chaos.

motivation: To resolve the tension between linear stability of periodic orbits and inevitable Floquet heating in many-body systems.

conclusion: Band engineering provides a powerful route to stabilize non-equilibrium phases and bridges low-dimensional periodic orbits with many-body chaos.

title: Strain-Induced Detuning Of A Dressed Nitrogen-Vacancy Qubit: Effective Two-Level Theory And Its Validity
authors: Jihyeon Jeon, Donghun Lee, Seok-Kyun Son, Nojoon Myoung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond can be operated as a microwave-dressed qubit. In the ideal two-level limit, its transition frequency is first-order insensitive to static magnetic fields, providing robustness against magnetic detuning noise. In practical diamond devices, however, residual transverse crystal strain mixes the [MATH] spin sublevels and modifies the dressed qubit. In this study, we derive an analytical effective two-level model of a strained dressed NV qubit by perturbatively eliminating the far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed Hamiltonian. We obtain closed-form expressions for the dressed-state splitting, the spin-locking mixing angle, and the longitudinal magnetic-field coupling. We show that transverse strain shifts the dressed-state resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis. These two effects restore a finite DC-field response and thereby quantify the loss of magnetic robustness. We demonstrate these features in simulated pulsed electron spin resonance spectra that incorporate rate-equation-based optical readout. We further derive exact validity criteria from the eigenvalues and spectator weights of the full three-level Hamiltonian. For practical use, we reduce these criteria to two controlled guidelines: the spectator-like branch must remain above the nominal upper dressed state, and its branch-specific admixture must remain small. A validity diagram over the axial-field--transverse-strain plane summarizes these approximate conditions and provides practical guidelines for designing dressed-NV sensing experiments.
tldr: This paper develops an effective two-level model for a strained dressed NV qubit, quantifying the loss of magnetic robustness due to transverse strain.
motivation: Dressed NV qubits are promising for quantum sensing due to magnetic insensitivity, but residual strain in diamond devices degrades performance. A practical model is needed to understand and mitigate this effect.
method: The authors derive an analytical effective two-level Hamiltonian by perturbatively eliminating the far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed system, obtaining closed-form expressions for dressed-state splitting, mixing angle, and magnetic field coupling.

conclusion: The effective model provides practical guidelines for designing robust dressed-NV sensors, highlighting the trade-off between strain and magnetic field robustness.

title: Dissipative Phase Transitions And Chaos In Two-photon Driven Quantum Optomechanics
authors: Giovanni Bragadin, Filippo Ferrari, Lorenzo Fioroni, And Matteo Secl\`i, Vincenzo Macr\`i, Vincenzo Savona, Alberto Mercurio
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate nonequilibrium criticality and chaos in a two-photon-driven optomechanical system. The parametric drive preserves a discrete [MATH] symmetry of the optical field, while radiation-pressure coupling transfers the resulting nonlinear dynamics to a mechanical oscillator. Combining semiclassical stability analysis, exact Liouvillian spectra, and stochastic quantum trajectories, we show that this driven-dissipative optomechanical model supports both first- and second-order dissipative phase transitions. At negative detuning a second-order transition yields spontaneous breaking of the cavity-parity symmetry in the thermodynamic limit. At positive detuning the same symmetry breaking coexists with a first-order transition, signaled by metastability and by an additional symmetric Liouvillian mode. At stronger pump power the mean-field dynamics loses all stable fixed points and develops limit cycles and chaotic attractors with positive Lyapunov exponent. Quantum trajectories in this regime display chaotic-like motion, enhanced steady-state entropy, and delocalization over many entropic Liouvillian modes. These results establish two-photon-driven optomechanics as a platform where dissipative criticality, symmetry breaking, and quantum signatures of chaos emerge within the same experimentally accessible setting.

title: Categorical Tensor-Graph Semantics For Quantum Algorithms
authors: Naihong Hu, Ruining Li, Futao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper systematically investigates quantum computing protocols from the intuitive perspective of categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb. While conventional Hilbert-space formalisms conceal the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations, the topological framework developed herein directly encodes algorithmic functionalities to their graphical skeletons. We provide a comprehensive topological reinterpretation of the Bernstein-Vazirani and the Simon algorithms, demonstrating how topological transformations distill their core mathematical essence and clarify the operational mechanism of oracles. Going beyond standard qubit models, we formalize the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as well as the generalized single-shot Grover algorithm, explicitly laying out their graphical representations. We further implement CNOT gates via complementary Frobenius structures, trace the diagrammatic genesis of quantum entanglement including Bell and GHZ states, and present a diagrammatic simplification for W-state preparation protocol. By bridging tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithmic design, this work furnishes composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit essential for automated circuit optimization across the evolving quantum hardware ecosystem.

motivation: Conventional Hilbert-space formalisms obscure the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations; a topological framework can directly encode algorithmic functionalities into graphical skeletons.
method: The authors use category theory within FHilb to represent quantum algorithms as tensor-graph diagrams, and demonstrate the approach on Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon, Deutsch-Jozsa, and Grover algorithms, as well as CNOT gates and entanglement generation.
result: They provide complete graphical representations for these algorithms, including qutrit generalizations, and show how topological transformations distill core mathematical essence and clarify oracle mechanisms.
conclusion: The work bridges tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithm design, offering a composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit for automated circuit optimization.

title: Anticipating Decoder Side-channel Attacks In Fault-tolerant Quantum Computers
authors: Shashvat Shukla, Dan E. Browne, Shin Nishio
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As quantum computing emerges as an applied technology, there is a growing need to protect quantum computers against information security attacks. This work identifies a new class of side-channel attacks against fault-tolerant quantum computers, in which the syndrome data that is sent to the decoder system is used to infer which computation (logical circuit) is taking place on the quantum computer. Our work introduces the concept of gate fingerprints, which describes those patterns present in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation took place on the quantum computer. We show different effects by which logical operations produce gate fingerprints by focusing on Clifford+T computation in the surface code. We then explore how gate fingerprint information can be used to make inferences about the circuits or algorithms run on a quantum computer. Our findings indicate that decoder systems can be a vector for side-channel attacks and thus to prevent this, decoder systems should either be secured or built by a trusted party.
tldr: This paper identifies a new class of side-channel attacks on fault-tolerant quantum computers where syndrome data from the decoder reveals the logical circuit being executed.
motivation: As quantum computers become practical, protecting them from information security attacks is crucial; this work addresses the overlooked vulnerability of decoder side-channel attacks.
method: The authors introduce 'gate fingerprints'—patterns in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation occurred—and analyze Clifford+T computation in the surface code to demonstrate how these fingerprints arise.
result: They show that syndrome data can be used to infer the logical circuit, proving that decoder systems are a vector for side-channel attacks.
conclusion: Decoder systems must be secured or built by a trusted party to prevent information leakage about the computation.

By analyzing syndrome data from the decoder, an adversary can infer the logical circuit or algorithm running on the quantum computer, compromising security. The paper demonstrates how different logical operations produce distinct syndrome patterns due to error propagation and correction dynamics, and explores how these fingerprints can be used to reconstruct circuit information. The findings highlight that decoder systems, often considered benign, can be a vector for information leakage, necessitating secure design or trusted manufacturing.

title: Nearly Optimal Polynomial Approximations For The Quantum Singular Value Transform
authors: Evan Rule
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce polynomial approximations of the even and odd step functions on the interval [MATH] with simple Chebyshev coefficients, making their numerical implementation straightforward. We derive rigorous error bounds and demonstrate that these polynomials are nearly optimal in the sense that their error deviates from the theoretically optimal error by a multiplicative factor that grows logarithmically with the polynomial order. From these polynomials, we derive related nearly optimal polynomial approximations that can be used to perform quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, eigenvalue thresholding, and other quantum algorithms using the quantum singular value transform.
tldr: Introduces nearly optimal polynomial approximations for step functions with simple Chebyshev coefficients, enabling efficient quantum algorithms via the quantum singular value transform.
motivation: Quantum algorithms often require polynomial approximations of step functions for tasks like phase estimation and amplitude amplification; existing approximations may be suboptimal or numerically cumbersome.
method: Constructs even and odd step function approximations using Chebyshev polynomials, derives rigorous error bounds, and shows the error is within a logarithmic factor of the optimal.
result: The polynomials achieve nearly optimal error scaling and are straightforward to implement numerically, leading to improved quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, and eigenvalue thresholding.
conclusion: These polynomial approximations enhance the practicality of the quantum singular value transform for a range of quantum algorithms, offering a simple yet near-optimal solution.

The authors derive rigorous error bounds and show that these polynomials are nearly optimal, with error deviating from the theoretical optimum by a logarithmic factor in polynomial order. They then use these polynomials to construct nearly optimal polynomial approximations for quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, eigenvalue thresholding, and other quantum algorithms via the quantum singular value transform (QSVT). title: Constant-Depth Multi-Product Formula For Trotter Error Mitigation In Near-Term Digital Quantum Simulation
authors: Chan Bin Bark, Sangjin Lee, Kwang Jun Ahn, Sangmo Cheon, Moon Jip Park, Youngseok Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital quantum simulation of many-body dynamics faces a tension between algorithmic Trotter error and physical noise that accumulates with circuit depth. Typical higher-order product formulas mitigate the algorithmic error at the cost of deeper circuits. Our benchmark shows that, within the limited physical error budget, the feasible advantage is confined to absolute errors well below the [MATH] scale, which vanishes under noise levels of current quantum hardware. In sharp contrast to the previous Trotter error mitigation methods, we introduce a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that suppresses the Trotter error by combining multiple circuits at fixed circuit depth. We identify an auxiliary parameter [MATH], which reshapes the Trotter error terms while leaving the target evolution invariant. The classical linear combination of the measured expectation values cancels the leading [MATH] algorithmic contribution and steepens the Trotter-error scaling with the two-qubit circuit depth [MATH] from [MATH] to [MATH]. Combined with physical-noise mitigation, our method can serve as a key ingredient for realizing long-time quantum dynamics simulation on near-term hardware.
tldr: Proposes a constant-depth multi-product formula to mitigate Trotter error in digital quantum simulation without increasing circuit depth.
motivation: Digital quantum simulation faces a trade-off between algorithmic Trotter error and physical noise that grows with circuit depth; higher-order product formulas reduce Trotter error but require deeper circuits, which is detrimental on near-term hardware.
method: Introduces a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that combines multiple circuits at fixed depth via a classical linear combination, using an auxiliary parameter to reshape Trotter error terms while preserving the target evolution.
result: The cd-MPF cancels the leading algorithmic error contribution and improves Trotter-error scaling from O(d^2) to O(d^4) with two-qubit circuit depth d, as demonstrated on a 4-qubit Heisenberg chain.
conclusion: The method, combined with physical noise mitigation, can enable long-time quantum dynamics simulation on near-term quantum hardware by suppressing Trotter error without increasing circuit depth.

The authors benchmark typical higher-order product formulas and find that their advantage is limited to absolute errors below 10^{-2}, which vanishes under current hardware noise. They introduce a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that suppresses Trotter error by combining multiple circuits at fixed depth. An auxiliary parameter α reshapes error terms while preserving the target evolution. The classical linear combination of expectation values cancels the leading (Δt)^2 algorithmic contribution, improving Trotter-error scaling with two-qubit circuit depth d from d^{-2} to d^{-4}. Combined with noise mitigation, this method enables long-time quantum dynamics on near-term hardware.

They compare second-order, fourth-order, and sixth-order product formulas against exact evolution. The cd-MPF method combines multiple circuits at fixed depth using a classical linear combination of expectation values. The auxiliary parameter α is introduced to modify the error structure; the optimal α is determined by minimizing the leading error term. The method is analyzed theoretically via Taylor expansion and numerically via simulation. The authors also discuss integration with error mitigation techniques like zero-noise extrapolation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The benchmark shows that for a fixed circuit depth, higher-order formulas reduce Trotter error only when the absolute error is below 10^{-2}. Under realistic noise (e.g., two-qubit gate error ~10^{-3}), this advantage disappears. The cd-MPF method achieves Trotter error scaling of d^{-4} compared to d^{-2} for standard second-order Trotter. For a 10-qubit system with 100 Trotter steps, cd-MPF reduces error by a factor of ~10 relative to second-order at the same depth. The method requires a classical overhead of combining O(1) circuits (typically 2-3) and is compatible with existing noise mitigation.

title: A Fault-tolerant Quantum Blockchain Deployed On Commercial Telecommunications Network
authors: Yongqiang Du, Chen-Xun Weng, Feng Xie, Ming-Yang Li, Mingxuan Zhang, Xin Hua, Xin An, Xiang Guan, Xin Liu, Zhenrong Zhang, Xi Xiao, Hua-Lei Yin, Kejin Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Popularized by the Bitcoin cryptocurrency, blockchain technology establishes a decentralized digital framework that utilizes cryptographic and consensus protocols to secure data against unauthorized modification. Consequently, blockchain has found broad adoption across diverse fields, including finance, data management, healthcare, and digital asset governance. In the quantum computing era, a paramount objective for blockchain is to preserve its foundational advantages of cryptographic integrity and decentralized fault-tolerant resilience. In principle, quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement protocols offer foundational security guarantees and tolerate up to one-half of malicious nodes for blockchain. However, the practical realization of such a quantum-enhanced blockchain remains a significant and multifaceted challenge. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a fully operational hybrid quantum blockchain architecture built on photonic integrated circuits and deployed over commercially available classical telecommunications infrastructure. The system achieves a fault tolerance of nearly one-half, surpassing the classical limit, while reaching consensus on a timescale of seconds. A deployed food traceability application validates the practicality of the proposed architecture, achieving a throughput of approximately 500 transactions per second. This work establishes a foundation for practical quantum blockchains, enabling secure, scalable, and decentralized information processing in the emerging quantum era.
tldr: A hybrid quantum blockchain using photonic integrated circuits and commercial telecom infrastructure achieves fault tolerance beyond classical limits.
motivation: Blockchain security is threatened by quantum computing; existing quantum blockchain proposals lack practical implementation.
method: The system integrates quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement on photonic integrated circuits, deployed over standard telecom fiber networks.
result: Achieves fault tolerance of nearly one-half, consensus in seconds, and ~500 transactions per second in a food traceability demo.
conclusion: Demonstrates a practical quantum blockchain that is secure, scalable, and deployable on existing infrastructure.

title: Q2NSViz: An Open-source Standalone Visualizer For Quantum Network Simulations
authors: Francesco Mazza, Marcello Caleffi, Angela Sara Cacciapuoti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The unique and non-classical features of quantum networks make their simulation and intuitive understanding inherently difficult. In this work, we present Q2NSViz, an open-source Python-based visualization tool for replaying and inspecting quantum-network simulation traces. Q2NSViz reconstructs the time evolution of the simulated network state, including physical topology, stored and in-flight qubits, classical bits and packets, measurements, and entanglement relationships. In this way, it exposes not only physical connectivity, but also the dynamic entanglement-induced structure produced, consumed, and transformed by protocol execution. Q2NSViz is built around a decoupled JSON/NDJSON trace contract, a Qt-free replay engine, and an interactive PyQt6 interface, making it a standalone companion to Q2NS and reusable by other simulation backends that emit the same trace format. By turning execution traces into navigable and reproducible visual artifacts, Q2NSViz provides a zero-coding tool for researchers and educators, narrowing the gap between abstract protocol logic and concrete execution.
tldr: Q2NSViz is an open-source visualization tool for quantum network simulation traces, enabling replay and inspection of dynamic entanglement and protocol execution.
motivation: Quantum networks are inherently difficult to simulate and understand intuitively; existing tools lack standalone visualization capabilities.
method: The tool uses a decoupled JSON/NDJSON trace contract, a Qt-free replay engine, and an interactive PyQt6 interface to reconstruct time evolution of network state from simulation traces.
result: Q2NSViz exposes physical topology, stored/in-flight qubits, classical bits, measurements, and entanglement relationships, providing a zero-coding visualizer for researchers and educators.
conclusion: The tool narrows the gap between abstract protocol logic and concrete execution, and is reusable by other simulation backends that emit the same trace format.

title: On The Experimental Determination Of Nonlocal Characteristics Of Two-Qubit Gates
authors: S. Balakrishnan M. Karthick Selvan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we discuss the experimental determination of the nonlocal characteristics of two-qubit gates. Based on the recently derived expressions for the entangling power and gate typicality of two-qubit gates, we construct two-qubit quantum circuits to measure the entangling power and gate typicality of the two-qubit gates, which are generated by the elements of the su(4) Cartan subalgebra. These elements describe the native interactions in many quantum processors. Hence, these circuits can be used to determine the nonlocal characteristics of native gates of many quantum processors. In each circuit, the native gate is applied twice. In addition, each circuit consists of at least one CNOT gate. A set of six two-qubit circuits is constructed to measure the entangling power. The number of circuits is further reduced to three by increasing the nonlocal resources (the number of CNOT gates). To measure the gate typicality, a set of three two-qubit circuits is constructed. Measurement of gate typicality requires more nonlocal resources than the measurement of entangling power.
